name: Habeas Corpus
statement: A detained person can demand that a court examine whether their imprisonment is lawful.
meaning: Habeas corpus is a legal recourse, the writ of habeas corpus, by which a person who is detained can challenge the lawfulness of their detention before a court. The writ compels the custodian, a jailer or the state, to bring the prisoner before the court and justify the imprisonment; the Latin means you shall have the body, in the sense of produce the body for examination. Crucially, it tests only whether the detention is lawful, not whether the prisoner is guilty of any crime. Often called the Great Writ, it is one of the oldest and most important safeguards of individual liberty against arbitrary or unlawful imprisonment. Rooted in English common law and codified in the Habeas Corpus Act of 1679, it stands as a fundamental check on the power of the state.
mechanism: The writ operates as a demand for justification. When a person is detained, they or someone on their behalf can petition a court, which issues the writ ordering the custodian to produce the prisoner and state the legal grounds for holding them. If the detention is found unlawful, the court orders release. Because it tests the legality of the detention rather than guilt or innocence, it is a procedural safeguard, not a substantive defence to a charge. Its force is such that constitutions protect it: the United States Constitution's Suspension Clause provides that the privilege of the writ shall not be suspended unless in cases of rebellion or invasion the public safety may require it, and even then suspension is exceptional, as when Abraham Lincoln suspended it during the American Civil War.

examples.text: The writ orders whoever holds a prisoner to bring them before a court and justify the detention, testing its legality rather than the prisoner's guilt.
The United States Constitution forbids suspending the writ except in cases of rebellion or invasion when public safety requires, a rare and grave exception.
Abraham Lincoln suspended habeas corpus during the American Civil War, a famous and controversial instance of the extreme circumstances in which it can be curtailed.

variants.name: The Habeas Corpus Act 1679
variants.text: The English statute that codified the procedure, strengthening the writ as a protection against unlawful detention and shaping its later constitutional forms.

variants.name: Suspension of the writ
variants.text: The exceptional curtailment of habeas corpus permitted only in cases of rebellion or invasion when public safety demands, as under the United States Suspension Clause.

whyItMatters: Habeas corpus is one of the oldest and most important protections of personal liberty and a foundational check on executive and state power. By letting anyone detained force a court to justify their imprisonment, it guards against arbitrary and indefinite detention, secret imprisonment, and abuse of authority, giving the courts a means to enforce the rule of law over the jailer. Its constitutional protection in many countries, and the strict limits on suspending it, reflect its status as the Great Writ, a bulwark of freedom against the state. Debates over its reach continue to arise wherever governments detain people outside ordinary criminal process.

working.text: petition a court for the writ to force whoever holds a prisoner to produce them and prove the detention is lawful.
use the writ to challenge whether the detention itself is lawful, not to determine guilt or innocence of any offence.
treat suspension as an extreme measure permitted only in rebellion or invasion when public safety requires, and resist its casual use.

limits: Habeas corpus tests only the lawfulness of detention, not guilt or innocence, so it is a procedural safeguard rather than a defence to a charge. It can be suspended in extreme circumstances, rebellion or invasion, when public safety requires, as Lincoln's Civil War suspension shows, and its practical strength depends on independent courts willing to enforce it against the government. Its scope over detentions outside ordinary criminal process, such as wartime or immigration detention, has been repeatedly contested. And while Magna Carta is often cited as a precursor, the writ actually predates it, tracing to earlier English practice, so its exact origins are older and more diffuse than the popular story suggests.
misreadings: Habeas corpus does not decide guilt or innocence; it tests only whether a detention is lawful, so it is not a trial or a substantive defence. It is a procedural remedy, not a guarantee of release, since a lawful detention will be upheld. And although Magna Carta of 1215 is often called its origin, the writ predates Magna Carta, so treating the charter as its source is a simplification; the protection developed through English common law over centuries.
origin: Rooted in English common law predating Magna Carta and codified by the Habeas Corpus Act of 1679, and protected in the United States by the Constitution's Suspension Clause; long known as the Great Writ of liberty.
